articles.title: How to Design Environments for Understanding Model Motives

curriculum.summary: This article explains the importance of understanding model motives in AI safety, particularly in distinguishing between benign and malign motivations. It introduces five design principles for creating environments to investigate model motives, including having uncertain causes, maximizing surprise, and avoiding implicit nudges. The article assumes basic knowledge of AI safety and model alignment concepts.
learning_outcomes: Understand the importance of model motive understanding in AI safety
Learn how to design environments to investigate model motives
Recognize the challenges of distinguishing between benign and malign motivations
strategic_questions: How can we effectively distinguish between benign and malign model motivations?
What are the implications of model motive understanding for AI safety and alignment?
How can we apply the design principles for environment creation to real-world AI safety scenarios?

articles.title: Schelling Goodness, and Shared Morality as a Goal

curriculum.summary: This article explores the concept of Schelling goodness, a notion that refers to a class of hypothetical coordination games where participants aim to converge on a moral verdict. It assumes knowledge of moral philosophy, game theory, and coordination games, and builds on these concepts to discuss the idea of shared morality as a goal. The article presents a thought-provoking exploration of what a large class of agents would say about moral questions, using only broadly shared constraints and common knowledge.
learning_outcomes: Understand the concept of Schelling goodness and its relation to shared morality
Learn how to apply game theory and coordination games to moral philosophy
Recognize the importance of common knowledge and broadly shared constraints in moral verdicts
Analyze the implications of Schelling goodness for AI safety and alignment
strategic_questions: How can Schelling goodness be used to align AI systems with human values?
What are the limitations of using coordination games to determine moral verdicts?
Can Schelling goodness be applied to real-world scenarios, and if so, how?
